Texas had an estimated **28,635,442 people**, based on the 2020 ACS 5-year release (2016–2020).

- I added up all 18,638 census block groups in the state.
- This is a survey estimate averaged over 2016–2020, so it has sampling error. It's not a count for one particular year, and it's not the 2020 Census count.
- I took "Texas" to mean the state. If you meant Texas County, Missouri, or Texas County, Oklahoma, I can look either of those up instead.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, summed over block groups with GEOID prefix 48.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01001 (Sex by Age). The 65+ count is male fields B01001e20–e25 plus female fields B01001e44–e49. The total is B01001e1. Both were summed over block groups by state.

I can't give you an exact figure, because this dataset only publishes median household income for each block group, and medians can't be combined into a county median. Using King County's 2020 release (2016–2020), my best estimate is **about $99,300**. That is approximate.

I estimated it three ways:

| Approach | Value (2020 dollars) |
|---|---|
| **Median worked out from the county's income ranges** (best estimate) | **≈ $99,300** |
| Average of the block-group medians, weighted by number of households | ≈ $108,500 |
| Average (mean) household income: total income ÷ households | ≈ $134,700 |

**How the best estimate works:**
- I added up all 900,061 King County households by income range.
- The middle household falls near the top of the $75,000–$99,999 range.
- I estimated a figure within that range, assuming households are spread evenly across it, which gives about $99,300. As a check, 49.7% of households (447,044) earn $100,000 or more, so the median should sit just under $100,000.

**Why the other two numbers are higher:**
- The mean is pulled up by high earners: 170,181 households make $200,000 or more.
- The weighted average of block-group medians is only a rough stand-in for a true county median.

All of these are survey estimates and carry sampling error.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), King County (block groups starting with 53033), summed over block groups:
- B19001 (Household Income), fields B19001e1–B19001e17
- B19025 (Aggregate Household Income), field B19025e1
- B19013 (Median Household Income), field B19013e1

The 2020 ACS 5-year release (2016–2020) estimates that Harris County has **1,795,219 housing units**.

| Occupancy | Housing units | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Occupied | 1,635,749 | 91.1% |
| Vacant | 159,470 | 8.9% |
| **Total** | **1,795,219** | 100% |

There are more housing units than households because some units are empty. The number of occupied units is exactly the same as the household count from before, since in the ACS each occupied unit is one household. The vacant count covers every kind of empty unit, such as homes for rent or sale and seasonal homes. These numbers are survey estimates, so they have some sampling error.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B25001 (Housing Units), field B25001e1, and B25002 (Occupancy Status), fields B25002e2 and B25002e3, summed over block groups in Harris County (GEOID prefix 48201).

In Cook County, IL, **20.3% of households** had income under $25,000 in the 2019 release, compared with **19.2%** in the 2020 release. That's a drop of about 1.1 percentage points.

| Release | Survey years | Total households | Households under $25,000 | Share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019 | 2015–2019 | 1,972,108 | 401,095 | 20.3% |
| 2020 | 2016–2020 | 1,991,474 | 382,543 | 19.2% |
| Change | | +19,366 | −18,552 | −1.1 pts |

**How to read this:**
- **The two periods overlap.** Both releases are 5-year estimates that share four of their five survey years (2016–2019). So this isn't a clean change from one year to the next. It mostly reflects swapping 2015 out for 2020. The Census Bureau recommends comparing periods that don't overlap.
- **The dollar amounts differ slightly.** Each release uses its own inflation-adjusted dollars: $25,000 in 2019 dollars for one and $25,000 in 2020 dollars for the other. Inflation between those years was small, but the cutoffs aren't exactly the same.
- **The numbers have some uncertainty.** These are survey estimates added up from block groups, so a change this small should be treated as approximate.

Source: ACS 2019 5-year (2015–2019) and ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B19001 (Household Income in the Past 12 Months). Fields: B19001e1 (total households) and B19001e2–e5 (under $10,000 through $20,000–$24,999), added up across Cook County block groups (GEOID prefix 17031).
